title: Quantifying Deep Groundwater Contributions to Streamflow With Inequality‐Constrained EEMMA From Sparse Isotope Series in Alpine Permafrost Basins
content:
Abstract

In alpine permafrost basins, dry-season runoff largely depends on subpermafrost groundwater (BPG, deep groundwater), yet cryohydrogeological conditions are complicated by time-varying hydrothermal regimes. Combined with the storage and regulation effects of permafrost on runoff, hydrograph-based estimates of the fractional contribution of BPG to streamflow (f BPG) are limited in validity and accuracy, and f BPG has not been fully quantified—particularly intra-annually. Here we leverage ensemble end-member mixing analysis (EMMA) and extend it to a non-negative inequality-constrained least squares (LSEI) framework suited to sparse-sample estimation with incomplete end members. Using the covariance structure of δ18O time series in precipitation, stream water, glacier and snow meltwater, and suprapermafrost groundwater, the approach resolves the contribution of the unknown end member, that is, BPG. The δ18O series undergo temporal harmonization, state-space smoothing, and collinearity screening prior to regression. Applied to the Three-River headwaters Region—a representative mid-latitude permafrost region—the method estimated ablation-season f BPG of 0.10 ± 0.02 to 0.17 ± 0.06, about 0.05 lower than the annual frozen-season flow fraction Q frozen/Q annual, consistent with additional shoulder-season recharge. Long-term (1961–2020) discharge records show slightly increasing Q frozen/Q annual, highlighting a gradually strengthening slow-reservoir role. The inferred BPG δ18O provided an isotopic baseline: winter stream water δ18O converged to it, diverged during ablation, and re-approached after events. Although ablation-season f BPG was modest, BPG sustained dry-season baseflow, underscoring the need to track f BPG for future water-security and climate-adaptation planning in degrading permafrost regions.
